items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the public health law, in relation to removing {123l} loflupane from the designation as a controlled substance
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S7306

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the public health law, in relation to removing {123l}
loflupane from the designation as a controlled substance

 PURPOSE :

To conform New York State statute to the federal controlled substance
act by exempting ioflupane.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section one of the bill removes {1231} ioflupane from the controlled
substance schedules.

Section two of the bill is the effective date.

 JUSTIFICATION :

{1231} ioflupane, the active ingredient in DaTscan, is an FDA-approved
radiopharmaceutical visual imaging agent that is used to help medical
practitioners differentiate between Parkinsonian syndromes and
essential tremors by allowing practitioners to capture detailed
pictures of the dopamine receptors in the brain.

The technique used to administer the test involves the injection of
DaTscan into a vein where it is then taken up by the brain's dopamine
receptors. The receptors can then be imaged through a form of MRI
scanning (single photon emission computed tomography, or SPECT) which
then makes it possible to determine whether there is a reduction in
function in the dopamine system, which usually occurs in the presence
of Parkinson's disease.

Parkinson's disease is a chronic, progressive neurological condition
that results from the degeneration of neurons in a region of the brain
that controls movement and for which there is currently no cure. It is
estimated that one million Americans are currently living with
Parkinson's disease, with approximately 60,000 new cases reported
annually, not including the thousands of cases that go undetected or
misdiagnosed.

There is currently no cure for Parkinson's disease, but optimal
treatment differs between Parkinsonian syndromes and other conditions
like essential tremor that mimic Parkinson's. Physicians use DaTscan
results to better differentiate between these conditions, which
benefits patients and can also help advance Parkinson's disease
research. Because of the miniscule amount of active ingredient in
DaTscan required to administer the test, as well as the presence of
radioactive material in the drug, it is effectively impossible to be
used or diverted for any narcotic or pharmacologic effects.

In 2011, the FDA approved the use of DaTscan as a diagnostic tool in
the detection of Parkinson's disease. In September 2015, the Federal
Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) subsequently removed DaTscan from the
Federal controlled substances list. However, because New York State
does not automatically make changes to the state's controlled
substances list when the DEA takes an action, DaTscan still remains a
Schedule II controlled substance in NYS. As a result of state and
federal procedures that must be followed by medical practitioners to
obtain DaTscan for use as a diagnostic tool, the use of DaTscan has
been severely limited in NYS because of its presence on the state's
controlled substances list. Other states that have adopted the federal
scheduling status have experienced a dramatic expansion in patient

access, particularly in areas outside of major cities, because of the
immediate reduction in regulatory burden.

Because of its unique ability to help diagnose Parkinson's disease in
patients, it is important that NYS remove DaTscan from the controlled
substance list so that it may be more widely available for use by
medical practitioners to effectively diagnose, treat and research new
treatment alternatives for this serious medical condition.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

New bill

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

None

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This act shall take effect immediately.
